gap: Tighter leading: baseline-to-baseline pitch is 74 device px in A against 76 in B (about 2.7% less) at the same glyph size, so the paragraph block sits denser. A also has a slightly wider character advance: 'boat.' ends at about 1557 display px in A and about 1540 in B, which pushes 'she' down to the next line in A's second paragraph.
gapTheirs: B has no hanging margin for heading markers. The '#' and '##' sit on the body's left edge (x≈432 display), so the heading words start 35 px ('The Lighthouse') and 52 px ('What the sea keeps') to the right of the body text. That makes a stepped left edge that changes with heading level. A hangs the markers outside the column (x≈396 and ≈378), so every word of text starts on one line at x≈432.
verdict: Both put the same measure of about 64 characters on the same near-white paper, so the choice comes down to how the column holds its edge. A keeps one clean left rule and hangs its structure in the margin, the way a typeset page does. B pushes every heading word inward by its own marker, and the eye catches that jog at each section. B's extra 2 px of leading is nicer to read, but it doesn't make up for the broken left edge.

states.name: narrow
states.gap: The body face is lighter and narrower, at about 22px per character. On the same #F7F7F7 paper with a 64px pitch, that leaves about 42px of air under every line against A's roughly 40px. The block looks thinner and greyer, and the space starts to outweigh the ink instead of framing it. The right edge also stops at about 1664, leaving 256px on the right against 234px on the left, a 22px asymmetry that A (233 left / 235 right) doesn't have.
states.gapTheirs: The frame bleeds. The top corners are rounded (radius about 20px) and the backdrop shows through them, e.g. srgb(236,234,212) at (5,5) and a teal edge at top right, so the #F7F7F7 paper doesn't fill the viewport. The type is also set wider: about 22.7px per character against B's 22px on a similar 1452px measure (233→1685 vs 234→1664). That gives looser, gappier word shapes over a 63px line pitch, and the text block reads as a grid rather than a page.
states.verdict: Both pages use the same #F7F7F7 paper, about 65 characters to the line and roughly 63–64px line pitch, so the measure and calm are nearly identical. A breaks the illusion of paper: its rounded window corners let the desktop show through, and its wide-tracked monospace sets the prose out like a terminal log. B's lighter type makes the block a little anaemic, and its right margin is 22px wider than its left, but the page reads edge to edge as one continuous sheet. I'd rather sit in B for three hours, though not by much.

states.name: short
states.gap: The lines are a little tighter. Line pitch is 74 device px against A's 76, and paragraph gaps are 148 against 152, even though B's type is about 1.4% bigger (advance ≈25.9 vs 25.5 px). So the leading is about 4% tighter relative to the type (pitch/advance ≈2.86 vs 2.98). Because the column is the same width (right edge x≈2253 vs 2255), B fits about 63 characters per line to A's 64, and the second paragraph breaks one word earlier ('empty,' / 'and').
states.gapTheirs: The heading doesn't line up with the body text. A puts the '#' inline, so 'The' starts at x≈672 device px while every body line starts at x≈622. That's a 50 px (2-column) jog on the page's left edge, right at the top where the eye first lands. B hangs the '#' out in the margin at x≈571, so the heading words and the body share one edge at x=622.
states.verdict: Both are the same calm, centred column on near-white paper, with left and right margins within 5 px of each other, so this comes down to details. A breaks the one thing a writer's eye keeps coming back to: the left edge. Its '#' pushes the title two columns in, so the text looks ragged on the left before a word has been read. B keeps one clean left edge and pays a little for it: slightly cramped leading and bigger type in a column that's no wider, which you'd notice over a long session.
